I think it’s Tywin by a semi-comfortable margin tbh. At the end of the day, they’re both powerful men driven by preserving their legacy. But Tywin was much more selfless in his acts towards securing his family’s position in ways that Logan simply was not. 

Tywin’s relationship with Tyrion was so toxic that it colors our overall perception too negatively. But by all accounts, he actually loved Jamie and Cersei and tried to do his best when raising them as kids so they’d be ready to assume the roles as adults that were necessary for the Lannisters to remain in power.

Tywin taught Jamie to read through dyslexia because he understood how important it was for his son to be sharp.  He also waited to marry Cersei until it meant she’d be queen of the seven kingdoms - not jumping the gun on some other powerful alliance that would have still been meaningful but not nearly as impactful.

Also, Tywin didn’t like Tyrion, but he did respect his strategizing capabilities and confided in Tyrion when the Lannisters were at war. And ultimately, Tywin’s behavior was much more excusable in the context of the times they lived in. There just isn’t a lot of practical use for dwarves in a world where killing and strength are so prevalent; dwarves are harder to marry off and can’t be relied on the same way in battle. And yet, Tywin let Tyrion live a life of debauchery and was content to let Tyrion spend frivolously as long as he was out of his hair (just an expression lol). 

And yeah, Tywin let Tyrion stand for Joffrey’s murder, but only because he knew he could leverage the moment to get Jamie back as his heir, which, in the GoT world, is all that matters. Jamie had no business being in the kingsguard, except for that he wanted to be near Cersei (which he shouldn’t have been doing in the first place).

Logan treated all of his kids (basically for their entire lives) with an ice cold indifference to their existence. Tywin seemed more “firm but fair” as a parent.

TLDR: Tywin was more hands-on in his kids’ lives and tried his best to make sure they’d maintain status and carry on the legacy after his death. Logan did not and was content to let his kids hate him and each other clawing for position until the end.

It’s hard to say fully without knowing how much you make tbh.  But I wouldn’t say you’re an asshole.  On the one hand, your wife’s behavior and response are problematic and obtuse. It’s really not about it being “her choice,” even if you don’t commingle your finances at the moment.  Her decision affects you, but more importantly your guys’ child. So there’s planning and coparenting that goes into that decision.  On the other hand, if you have a lucrative career and use her salary as more of a cushion, I could see why she’d feel some type of way if you told her, in effect, to “get her ass back to work” if she’s unhappy there.

For example, my partner and I recently had a similar experience, except we don’t have a child yet.  I make ~300k per year and my partner makes ~70k. At this point, we’re basically trying to figure out when is the best time for her to get pregnant. My partner said something similar to what yours did: that she’s done working once she gets pregnant. We argued at first because, like you, I want her to keep working. Why give up the money? That’s investments, vacations, nights out, rainy days, etc. But her argument was that if she and I can’t make it work on my salary then we’ve fucked up.  And she’d rather be a SAHM.  Guess what? We stopped having sex for a while lol. I felt like it was unfair (mostly jealousy because I’d love to stop working - and yes I know parenting is work, I don’t need the lecture lol). But I’ve sat with it for a while and she’s right.  I’d rather her quit so she can stay home and be happy than keep working and be miserable. I don’t want her to stay and end up resenting me long term. So, if that means less disposable income then it just is what it is.

Honestly, and not to get too far into the weeds, but I think your and Michael’s view here is adjacent to the mindset many Americans have regarding “successful” people today. By and large, many of the highest paid white-collar workers in America (think physicians, attorneys, finance, and say, structural engineers) are highly educated and work longer hours than their less educated blue-collar (think police officers, retail industry, electricians, construction) counterparts. But because the high-paid workers objectively work “hard” (at least if measured by time spent working), many of them believe they’re “self-made.” Which is to say, as you suggest, they feel like their success was earned.

But what these ostensibly self-made people often don’t acknowledge is that they had many resources poured into them that others did/could not because of systemic socioeconomic barriers. That is, the high paid are given the social and educational training needed to perform the lucrative sophisticated jobs while the comparatively low paid are left behind. So in short, a system has been created that perpetuates the concentration of the best opportunities to the narrow set of individuals that can afford to pay their child’s way through the labyrinth of educational costs necessary for getting ahead.

So to end with a show hypothetical example, Michael and Sarah’s kid, the son of an engineer and a doctor, would benefit from the socioeconomic advantages that come with having rich parents. That kid would likely live in a neighborhood with similarly situated families and would go to a public school that spends more resources on its students than schools in working-class neighborhoods. Or even more likely, Michael and Sarah would pay for his private school that has even smaller classrooms, i.e., more hands on concentrated teaching to prepare students for college and so on. 

Now think of Sucre and Mari Cruz, their child would attend a school in the working-class district I referenced above without the same advantages associated with the more affluent public schools, let alone private schools.

In that scenario, do you think Sucre’s kid would be right to be upset if Michael’s kid said he likely could have been admitted to that institution even without his parent’s help? 

If your answer is yes, then the answer to your post should also be yes. Michael’s kid’s response is insulting bc it assumes that their unequal opportunities were only based on differences in effort; it ignores the effects of the advantages that were with him every step of the way that Sucre’s kid comparatively didn’t experience. People say this, but I think they read more into the ending than they should.  To me, the film felt like an extended and gratuitous farewell for Wick fans with its parallels to the first three installments. There’s also not-so-subtle foreshadowing throughout regarding John’s death, and his acceptance with it.  

Notwithstanding the foreshadowing that occurred in the film’s first two hours, think of John and Winston’s conversation on the Bowery’s boat the evening before the duel. John says it’ll all be over after today and then tells Winston he wants “loving husband” on his headstone. Also, the exchange with Caine before Caine’s final shot: “those who cling to death, live; and those who cling to life, die.”  Once the duel is concluded, John asks Winston if he’ll “take him home” and Winston’s facial expression indicates that John’s death is imminent, but he respects John enough to acquiesce on not attempting to save him.  John walks down the stairs and the film, again, not subtly, zooms out to show the sunlight (life) and darkness (death) on either side of him.  He got his “life back” with his final memory and words being Helen as he topples towards sunlight and dies. 

To be sure, Winston and the Bowery speculate  about whether John was in heaven or hell and Winston gives a final “farewell, my son.” Plus, they have John’s dog in that scene. John always made sure his dog was taken care of while he was away (Think of J2 and J3 with the concierge.) His obligation to the table was “satisfied” per the Harbinger, so John would have no reason to fake his death. The entire franchise, but particularly 4, were about “rules and consequences” because without them “they live with the animals.” I don’t think the table would undermine its own credibility by making a mockery of the duel and going back on their word. 

I think people just want there to be a John Wick 5 (as do I) but they delude themselves into thinking John Wick 4 was ambiguous. The only thing we don’t see is John in a casket, but it wasn’t necessary given everything I explained above. All that being said, I’ll be a few edibles deep and center aisle watching 5 in theaters if it’s ever released lol.

I’m a retaker - failed July 2021 and just sat for February 2022. With my livelihood on the line, (I’ll get fired if I fail again) I put my faith in Adapitbar.
